The pulse-gating system is shown to have a far superior system noise figure compared to the CW-nulling system.
The pulse-gating system has only slightly greater system loss due to the added complexity of the pulse modulating and range gating components.
The combined effect is that the pulse-gating technique can improve signal-to-noise ratio and increase the reliability of accurate RCS measurements.
The pulse-gating system reduces the effect of chamber clutter sources by time-separating the target area from the surrounding chamber.
Time domain measurements show the relative amplitudes of various chamber scattering sources.
For high RCS targets, the CW-nulling and pulse-gating systems perform equally well, but for low RCS targets the pulse-gating system produces more accurate RCS patterns.
The CW-nulling system fails to distinguish between target and clutter source returns when the target RCS is of the same order as chamber clutter.
The pulse-gating system has the flexibility to perform both fixed frequency RCS versus aspect angle measurements and new stepped frequency or time-domain measurements.
The Nakagami-Rice distribution function describes the probability distribution of the measured RCS, which approaches Rayleigh as the clutter cross section decreases.
Clutter sources that may remain in the pulse-gating system include the target support pedestal, absorber cones, and target/support pedestal interactions.
The system sensitivity equation used is: (Pt*G^2*λ^2*σ)/(4π^3*kTo*B*Fs*R^4), where Fs is the system noise figure.
The CW-nulling system illuminates the entire chamber and cancels out the background clutter, but cannot distinguish between target and clutter returns.
The pulse-gating system time-separates the target area from the surrounding chamber, eliminating the most significant clutter sources.
When a target is introduced into the chamber, the field distributions change from the empty chamber case, causing the CW-nulling system to no longer accurately cancel the background clutter.
The pulse-gating system's ability to time-separate the target from chamber clutter leads to more accurate RCS measurements, especially for low RCS targets.
